name: Licensing and Professional Credentials for ADU Design Contractors
headline: Licensing and Professional Credentials for ADU Design Contractors
articleBody: ### Licenses and Qualifications for ADU Design Professionals In California, the **Contractors State License Board (CSLB)** regulates construction contracting, requiring a licensed general building contractor (typically a “B” classification) for most structural residential work beyond very small repairs. For design, California’s Architects Practice Act regulates who may call themselves an architect and requires a licensed architect for certain building types and complexities. For typical one- and two-family dwellings and their accessory structures, state law allows unlicensed designers to prepare plans, as long as they do not present themselves as architects and stay within residential scope. Building departments in Los Angeles County and its cities commonly accept drawings from licensed architects, engineers, or experienced residential designers, provided the documents meet professional drafting and code standards. When a contractor advertises ADU design services, homeowners should verify the **CSLB license status**, classifications, and any disciplinary actions using CSLB’s online license lookup. The California Department of Consumer Affairs encourages checking bond and workers’ compensation coverage, and confirming that the business name and license number match all contracts and marketing materials. For projects involving complex structural modifications—such as garage conversions with new second-story additions or hillside construction—local building authorities often encourage or require plans stamped by a California-licensed structural engineer or architect. Industry practice in Los Angeles ADU firms shows many teams bundling roles: licensed general contractors partner with in-house or external architects and engineers, or provide drafting services and then obtain engineering stamps as needed. When evaluating qualifications, homeowners should look for demonstrated ADU experience in the jurisdiction, familiarity with local zoning codes, and a track record of successful permit approvals, rather than relying solely on general residential construction experience.
